analysis.title: Ruminations - Macro, Micro, Markets: Feast and then famine
key_insights: The last 2-3 weeks were hard to trade. The index level held near highs while factor, sector, spread and theme volatility was large. Gross exposure lost money across regions and strategies.
Nasdaq fell over 6% in two weeks, with a semiconductor rout. Momentum fell about 15% in the same period. Credit instruments linked to the AI buildout traded at high velocity.

The GS risk indicator fell sharply over three weeks and is negative for the first time since March. Moves look technical and flow driven, and investors are waiting for a bottom to become evident rather than calling one.

Private equity reports on AI buildout financing and mark-to-market returns, plus a strategist report on productivity, are shifting corporate focus from token spend as a growth driver to token spend as a margin cost. Revenue per worker and profit margins are rising for the Mag 7 but flat for the S&P 493.

Middle East tension is pushing oil back toward its April/May highs. French civil unrest has pushed the OAT-Bund spread to an all-time high. Falling yields are viewed with less enthusiasm because they are tied to the AI unwind and possible capex slowing.

The author's key anchors are AI, oil and yields, now with credit and credit spreads, set against growth, employment and earnings. Market is broadening, rotating to defensives, real assets, quality and low leverage, and de-grossing. The author says it feels closer to the end than the beginning of the unwind.

This week's open questions are the Middle East path before the midterms, whether yields keep normalising, and whether Friday's AI reversion is a rebound or part of a deeper sell-off. The Meta news that morning is seen as a potential clearing event.

A large part of the S&P reports this week. Results so far have been solid with little reward. Three hyperscalers will give capex and ROI detail. Meta is selling off while raising capex and Tesla is selling off while cutting capex.
H1 treated all news as good news. H2 applies a higher bar and treats most news as bad. Fed hike probability moved from near certainty to around 75% over the last couple of weeks.
Seasonals: in 30 years the S&P has fallen in November only three times (2000 -8%, 2007 -4.4%, 2008 -7.48%). Five trading days remain before November.

Per Openrouter, token demand is up 27x since last November, with open-weight models at 72% of tokens. GPU rental prices are up YTD: H200 +160%, B200 +120%, H100 +35%, and the six-year-old A100 rents for more than at the start of the year. Bulls read this as demand broadening, bears read it as cost per token versus revenue per token moving the wrong way as open weight gains share.

Breadth: S&P 500 stocks above their 50-day average rose 5 points on Friday to 61%, the highest since August, and are up 17 points over three weeks while the S&P is roughly unchanged. The author reads the unwind as cleaning out positioning, reducing concentration and normalising multiples.

Private markets diverge from public markets. Exits (SpaceX, Cerebras, Cursor, Hugging Face) are large, concentrated and interdependent, and valuations are stepping up quickly while public markets are in an AI risk-off. The author expects the gap to be resolved through IPOs, which can be bumpy (examples Firmus, Oura).

Boom loop: hyperscaler capex drives AI ecosystem revenue, which draws venture and growth capital. The missing link is whether revenues persist without the capex anchor, and vendor financing blurs revenue and financing lines.

Charts: 22 Oct was the 5th largest de-grossing event this year, driven entirely by long selling, and the largest long selling since September 2025. US Quality is at 12-month highs. Momentum has given back all its 2026 gains versus the market.

macro_indicators.interpretation: Down from near certainty over the last couple of weeks. Lower hike odds are tied to the AI unwind and are not celebrated.
French civil unrest is widening the spread, a sign of rising political risk premium in French debt.
Re-escalating Middle East tension is pushing oil higher, one of the three core themes of 2026 with yields and AI.
Demand for AI compute is growing, with open-weight models at 72% of tokens. Both bulls and bears use it to support their argument.

risk_factors: Further de-grossing and momentum unwinds in a narrow, concentrated market.
AI capex slowing and its GDP impact, plus questions over who pays for the buildout and when revenues arrive.
Credit and credit spreads on instruments tied to the AI buildout, including vendor financing that blurs revenue and financing.
Middle East escalation pushing oil higher.
French political unrest and a record OAT-Bund spread.
A November drawdown. The author notes that a red November has tended to precede much larger losses.
A bumpy re-pricing of private AI valuations through IPOs.

tension_points.bull_case: Token demand is up 27x since last November and GPU rental prices are up YTD (H200 +160%, B200 +120%, H100 +35%), which the bulls read as demand broadening and the addressable market growing.
tension_points.bear_case: Cost per token versus revenue per token is moving the wrong way as open-weight models gain share (72% of tokens), so revenue may not cover the build cost.

tension_points.bull_case: The unwind has cleaned out positioning, reduced concentration and normalised multiples, with 61% of S&P 500 stocks above their 50-day average, which is healthy in the long term.
tension_points.bear_case: Broadening has hurt performance, since assets followed performance into a crowded, concentrated market, and investors are playing defense.

theme_stances.key_argument: Investors are de-grossing and playing defense, and the author says the unwind feels closer to the end than the beginning.
theme_stances.evidence: feels closer to the end than the beginning

theme_stances.key_argument: The market is still debating the cost of the build, who pays and how long revenues take, though demand is clearly growing.
